knowledge.title: Somali grammar at a glance / Naxwaha Af-Soomaaliga
knowledge.text:
Somali (Af-Soomaali) is an East Cushitic language of the Afro-Asiatic family. Standard Somali is based on the Northern dialect group and has been written in the official Latin script since 21 October 1972. Key facts an assistant must get right:
- Word order is verb-final (Subject-Object-Verb): "Cali bariis buu cunay" (Ali ate rice). Word order is flexible because focus particles, not position, show emphasis.
- Every main declarative clause normally carries ONE focus element: the particle waa (focus on the verb/whole statement), or baa / ayaa after a focused noun phrase, or the cleft waxaa. Subordinate clauses take no focus particle.
- Nouns have two genders (masculine, feminine), shown mainly by the definite suffix (-ka/-ga/-ha for masculine, -ta/-da/-sha for feminine) and by verb agreement. Gender is also carried by tone, which is not written (ínan "boy" vs inán "girl").
- Many nouns switch gender in the plural (gender polarity): buugga "the book" (m) but buugagta "the books" (f).
- Verbs agree with the subject in person, number and gender. Third-person feminine and second-person singular share the same form: "way keentay" (she brought) / "waad keentay" (you brought).
- Tense/aspect: present habitual, present progressive, simple past, past progressive, past habitual (with jir), future (infinitive + doon), conditional (infinitive + lahaa).
- Pronoun objects and prepositions are small clitics placed before the verb and fuse together: "ii keen" (bring me), "iiga warran" (tell me about it).
- Negation uses ma (statements), ha (prohibitions), aan (inside relative/subordinate clauses).
- Yes/no questions use ma (or miyaa): "Ma timid?" (Did you come?).
- Articles are suffixes, not separate words: nin (a man), ninka (the man), ninkii (the man already mentioned / that man of the past), ninkan (this man), ninkaas (that man).
Example sentence anatomy: "Faadumo shaah bay ii keentay." = Faadumo + tea + FOCUS(baa+ay 'she') + to-me + brought.FEM = "Faadumo brought me TEA." For an assistant: always match verb gender to the subject (Asli baa keentay, not *Asli baa keenay), keep exactly one focus marker per main clause, and never translate word-by-word from English order.
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_language; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Focus markers: waa, baa, ayaa, waxaa / Erayada xoojinta
knowledge.text:
Somali marks what is new or emphasised with focus particles. A normal main statement needs one of them.
1. waa – verb/statement focus (no noun singled out). It fuses with subject pronoun clitics:
| waa + aan (I) = waan | waa + aad (you sg/pl) = waad | waa + uu (he) = wuu | waa + ay (she/they) = way | waa + aannu (we excl.) = waannu | waa + aynu (we incl.) = waynu |
Examples: "Waan fahmay" (I understood). "Wuu yimid" (He came). "Way tagtay" (She left). With a noun predicate: "Cali waa macallin" (Ali is a teacher). "Waa run" (It's true).
2. baa – placed right AFTER the focused noun phrase. Fusions: baan, baad, buu, bay, baannu, baynu. "Shaah baan rabaa" (It's TEA I want). "Cali baa yimid" (ALI came). "Xamar buu u socdaa" (He is going to MOGADISHU).
3. ayaa – same function as baa, a little more formal/written, very common in news: ayaan, ayaad, ayuu, ayay, ayaannu, ayaynu. "Madaxweynaha ayaa sheegay..." (The PRESIDENT said...). "Maanta ayuu imanayaa" (He is coming TODAY).
4. waxaa – cleft "what ... is": fusions waxaan, waxaad, wuxuu, waxay, waxaannu, waxaynu. Very frequent in speech and writing; the focused item comes AFTER the verb. "Waxaan rabaa shaah" (What I want is tea / I want tea). "Wuxuu yiri: 'Waan imanayaa'" (He said: 'I'm coming'). "Waxaa yimid martida" (The guests came – presentational).
Rules and common errors:
- When a noun object is focused with baa/ayaa and the subject is a pronoun or a non-focused noun, the subject clitic is required: "Wiilkii moos buu cunay" (correct) vs *"Wiilkii moos baa cunay" (missing clitic). "Adigu moos baad cuntay" (correct), not *"moos baa cuntay".
- If the subject itself is focused, the verb shows reduced agreement: "Nimankii baa yimid" (the MEN came) is correct even though yimid is not plural. With focused feminine subject the verb still takes the -t- form: "Asli baa keentay".
- Negative statements use ma instead of waa: "Ma imanayo" (I'm not coming); negative focus: "Cali ma aha ee waa Axmed" (It's not Ali, it's Ahmed).
- Questions combine ma + focus: "Ma Cali baa yimid?" (Was it Ali who came?), "Miyaad timid?" (Did you come?).
- Do not stack two focus markers in one main clause (*"Waan shaah baan rabaa").
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/spec/grammar/0017-common-mistakes.md (CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Personal pronouns: independent, subject and object forms / Magacuyaallada
knowledge.text:
Somali has three sets of personal pronouns.
Independent (emphatic) pronouns – behave like nouns (with -u when they are a non-focused subject):
| I: aniga (anigu) | you sg: adiga (adigu) | he: isaga (isagu; also spelled asaga) | she: iyada (iyadu) |
| we (exclusive, not you): annaga (annagu) | we (inclusive, you too): innaga (innagu) | you pl: idinka (idinku) | they: iyaga (iyagu) |
Use: "Aniga ayaa keenay" (I brought it). "Adigu ma timid?" (Did YOU come?). Short forms used in speech: ani, adi (Southern/Maay also ani, adi).
Subject clitics – attached to focus words, conjunctions or verbs: aan (I), aad (you sg), uu (he), ay (she), aannu (we excl.), aynu (we incl.), aad (you pl), ay (they). They fuse: waan, waad, wuu, way, baan, buu, ayay, waxaan, hadduu ("if he"), markaad ("when you").
Object clitics – placed before the verb:
| i = me | ku = you (sg) | na = us (excl.) | ina = us (incl.) | idin = you (pl) |
There is no clitic for him/her/them (the third-person object is understood or expressed by a noun). Examples: "I caawi!" (Help me!), "Waan ku jecelahay" (I love you), "Wuu na arkay" (He saw us), "Waan idin sugayaa" (I am waiting for you pl.).
- Impersonal "la" (one/someone) acts as a passive: "Waa la keenay" (It was brought). "Halkan lagama sigaar cabbo" (One does not smoke here).
- Reflexive/reciprocal "is": "Is caawiya!" (Help each other!), "Waan is dhaqay" (I washed myself).
Inclusive vs exclusive "we": use innaga/aynu/ina when the listener is included ("Aynu tagno" – let's go, you and me) and annaga/aannu/na when the listener is excluded ("Annagu waannu tagaynaa, adiguna joog" – we are going, you stay). Northern and Southern usage both keep this distinction, though some speakers use annaga loosely. For an assistant speaking to a user about itself and the user together, prefer the inclusive forms ("Aynu eegno" – let's look).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Verb tenses and aspects overview with 'cun' (eat) / Amminada falka
knowledge.text:
Regular (suffixing) verbs add endings to the stem. Model verb: cun (eat), class I.
| Person | Present habitual | Simple past | Future |
| I (aan) | cunaa | cunay | cuni doonaa |
| you sg (aad) | cuntaa | cuntay | cuni doontaa |
| he (uu) | cunaa | cunay | cuni doonaa |
| she (ay) | cuntaa | cuntay | cuni doontaa |
| we (aannu/aynu) | cunnaa | cunnay | cuni doonnaa |
| you pl (aad) | cuntaan | cunteen | cuni doontaan |
| they (ay) | cunaan | cuneen | cuni doonaan |
Other aspects (3rd masc. shown; same person endings):
- Present progressive: cunayaa (is eating) – "Waan cunayaa" (I'm eating). 2sg/3f cunaysaa, 1pl cunaynaa, 2pl cunaysaan, 3pl cunayaan.
- Past progressive: cunayay (was eating) – "Wuu cunayay markaan imid" (He was eating when I came).
- Past habitual: cuni jiray (used to eat) – "Waxaan cuni jiray canjeero subax walba" (I used to eat canjeero every morning). 2sg/3f cuni jirtay, 1pl cuni jirnay, 2pl cuni jirteen, 3pl cuni jireen.
- Conditional/counterfactual: cuni lahaa (would have eaten).
- Future: infinitive (-i or -n) + doon: "Berri ayaan cuni doonaa". In everyday speech the present progressive often expresses near future: "Berri waan imanayaa" (I'm coming tomorrow).
- Subjunctive (in subordinate clauses, after ha/aan): ending -o: "inaan cuno" (that I eat), "Ha cuno" (let him eat).
Negatives of cun: ma cuno (don't eat, present), ma cunayo (am not eating), ma cunin (didn't eat – same for every person), ma cuni jirin (didn't use to), ma cuni doono (won't eat), ma cuni lahayn (wouldn't have eaten).
Spelling: the past ending -ay is also written -ey (cunay/cuney, sameeyay/sameeyey); both are seen. Sound rule: the -t- of 2sg/3f becomes -d- after some stems and assimilates (e.g., stems ending in l: "gal" → "gashaa" you enter; in "yeel" → "yeeshaa"), so do not mechanically paste -taa onto every stem; check known forms.
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/naxwe/08-hogatuska-baradigmaha-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Conjugation tables: tag (go), keen (bring), rab (want) / Falalka tag, keen, rab
knowledge.text:
tag – go/leave (class I). Full aspect table (subject: I / you sg / he / she / we / you pl / they):
- Present habitual: tagaa / tagtaa / tagaa / tagtaa / tagnaa / tagtaan / tagaan
- Present progressive: tagayaa / tagaysaa / tagayaa / tagaysaa / tagaynaa / tagaysaan / tagayaan
- Simple past: tagay / tagtay / tagay / tagtay / tagnay / tagteen / tageen
- Past progressive: tagayay / tagaysay / tagayay / tagaysay / tagaynay / tagayseen / tagayeen
- Past habitual: tagi jiray / tagi jirtay / tagi jiray / tagi jirtay / tagi jirnay / tagi jirteen / tagi jireen
- Future: tagi doonaa / tagi doontaa ...
Imperative: tag! (sg) / taga! (pl); negative: ha tegin / ha tegina. Note the vowel change in some forms (tegi, tegin alongside tagi) – both appear in writing. "Suuqa ayaan tagayaa" (I'm going to the market). "Halkee buu tagay?" (Where did he go?).
keen – bring (class I):
- Present: keenaa / keentaa / keenaa / keentaa / keennaa / keentaan / keenaan
- Past: keenay / keentay / keenay / keentay / keennay / keenteen / keeneen
- Progressive: keenayaa / keenaysaa / keenayaa / keenaysaa / keenaynaa / keenaysaan / keenayaan
- Future: keeni doonaa. Imperative: keen! / keena!; negative ha keenin / ha keenina.
"Biyo ii keen" (Bring me water). "Asli baa keentay" (ASLI brought it). "Ma keentay lacagta?" (Did you bring the money?)
rab – want (class I; doon is a common synonym, especially in the progressive "doonayaa"):
- Present: rabaa / rabtaa / rabaa / rabtaa / rabnaa / rabtaan / rabaan
- Past: rabay / rabtay / rabay / rabtay / rabnay / rabteen / rabeen
- Negative present: ma rabo (I/he), ma rabtid (you), ma rabto (she), ma rabno (we), ma rabtaan, ma rabaan; "Ma rabo" = I don't want (it).
"Maxaad rabtaa?" (What do you want?) "Waxaan rabaa inaan Xamar tago" (I want to go to Mogadishu) – note: want + "in" + subjunctive (-o/-no). "Ma doonaysaa shaah?" (Would you like tea?)
Assistant tip: "waan rabaa" alone sounds abrupt in service contexts; softer is "Waxaan jeclaan lahaa..." (I would like...).
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Conjugation: samee (do/make) and sii (give) – class II verbs / Falalka samee iyo sii
knowledge.text:
Class II verbs have imperatives ending in -i or -ee. Their endings add -y- / -s- / -n- linking consonants.
samee – do, make (class IIB, imperative -ee). Infinitive samayn (also spelled sameyn).
- Present: sameeyaa (I) / samaysaa (you) / sameeyaa (he) / samaysaa (she) / samaynaa (we) / samaysaan (you pl) / sameeyaan (they)
- Past: sameeyay or sameeyey / samaysay / sameeyay / samaysay / samaynay / samayseen / sameeyeen
- Progressive: samaynayaa / samaynaysaa / samaynayaa / samaynaysaa / samaynaynaa / samaynaysaan / samaynayaan
- Future: samayn doonaa. Past negative: ma samayn. Imperative: samee! (sg) / sameeya! (pl); prohibitive: ha samayn / ha samaynina.
Examples: "Maxaad samaynaysaa?" (What are you doing?) "Shaqadii waan sameeyay" (I did the work). "Cunto ma samaysay?" (Did you make food?) Spellings with -ay- and -ey- (samaysay/sameysay) both occur. Another verb of this pattern: caddee (make white/clarify; future caddayn doonaa; SLS lists the negative form caddaynin).
sii – give (class IIA, imperative -i). Infinitive siin.
- Present: siiyaa / siisaa / siiyaa / siisaa / siinnaa / siisaan / siiyaan
- Past: siiyay (siiyey) / siisay / siiyay / siisay / siinnay / siiseen / siiyeen
- Progressive: siinayaa / siinaysaa / siinayaa ...; Future: siin doonaa. Past negative: ma siin.
- Imperative: sii! / siiya!; prohibitive: ha siin.
Examples: "I sii biyo" (Give me water). "Lacagta ma siisay?" (Did you give him the money?) "Waan ku siin doonaa" (I will give it to you). Other IIA verbs: kari (cook): kariyaa, kariyey, karin doonaa (SLS); toosi (straighten), diyaari (prepare: "Cuntada diyaari" prepare the food), akhri (read: "Akhri!"), xusuusi (remind).
Distinguish sii (give) from the directional particle sii (onward/away from speaker): "Sii soco" (keep going), "Waan sii socdaa" (I'm on my way).
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Irregular prefix verbs: ahaan (be), imow/yimid (come), dheh/oran (say), aqoon (know), ool (be located) / Falalka horkabayaasha leh
knowledge.text:
Five very common verbs mark the person with PREFIXES (y-, t-, n-) instead of suffixes. They are irregular and must not be "regularised" (e.g., never *imoway for 'came').
ahaan – to be. Present: ahay (I) / tahay (you, she) / yahay (he) / nahay (we) / tihiin (you pl) / yihiin (they). Past: ahaa / ahayd / ahaa / ahayd / ahayn / ahaydeen / ahaayeen. Negative present: ma ihi / ma ihid / ma aha / ma aha / ma ihin / ma ihidin / ma aha; negative past: ma ahayn. Future: ahaan doonaa. Imperative: ahow/ahaw (sg), ahaada (pl): "Iga raalli ahow" (excuse me / be pleased with me). With adjectives the verb fuses: "Waan fiicanahay" (I am fine = fiican + ahay), "Way qurux badan tahay" (she is beautiful), "Wuu xanuunsan yahay" (he is ill). "Ma aha" also means "it isn't": "Sidaas ma aha" (That's not so).
imow – to come. Present: imaaddaa / timaaddaa / yimaaddaa / timaaddaa / nimaaddaa / timaaddaan / yimaaddaan. Past: imid (I) / timid (you, she) / yimid (he) / nimid (we) / timaaddeen (you pl) / yimaaddeen (they). Progressive (regular): imanayaa, imanaysaa... Future: iman doonaa. Negative: ma iman (didn't come), ma imaaddo (doesn't come), ma imanayo (isn't coming). Imperative: imow or kaalay (sg), imaada or kaalaya (pl). "Xaggee ayaad ka timid?" (Where did you come from?) "Waxaan ka imid Hargeysa." "Cali weli ma iman" (Ali hasn't come yet).
dheh / oran (odhan) – to say. Present: iraahdaa (idhaahdaa) / tiraahdaa / yiraahdaa / tiraahdaa / niraahdaa / tiraahdaan / yiraahdaan. Past: iri (idhi) / tiri (tidhi) / yiri (yidhi) / tiri / niri (nidhi) / tiraahdeen / yiraahdeen. Infinitive oran (odhan): future oran doonaa. Negative past: ma oran (ma odhan). Imperative: dheh (sg), dhaha (pl). "Maxaad tiri?" (What did you say?) "Wuxuu yiri waan imanayaa." The dh/r pairs (idhi/iri, odhan/oran) are Northern vs Southern-leaning spellings; both are accepted.
aqoon – to know. Present: aqaan / taqaan / yaqaan / taqaan / naqaan / taqaanniin / yaqaanniin. Past: iqiin / tiqiin / yiqiin / tiqiin / niqiin / tiqiinneen / yiqiinneen. Negative: ma aqaan (I don't know), ma aqoon (didn't know). "Ma aqaan" is the standard "I don't know"; "Ma garanayo" (I can't tell/recognise) is also common.
ool – to be located (mainly 3rd person): yaal (he/it m.), taal (she/it f.), yaalliin (they); past yiil / tiil. "Furayaashu xaggee bay yaalliin?" (Where are the keys?)
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/naxwe/08-hogatuska-baradigmaha-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Imperatives, requests and 'let's' / Amarka iyo codsiga
knowledge.text:
Positive imperative:
- Class I (stem ends in consonant): singular = bare stem, plural adds -a. keen / keena (bring), tag / taga (go), cun / cuna (eat), qor / qora (write), fadhiiso (sit, class III) / fadhiista, sug / suga (wait).
- Class II: samee / sameeya (do), sii / siiya (give), akhri / akhriya (read), kari / kariya (cook).
- Class III (middle verbs) end in -o / -so: joogso (stop!), qabso (take hold), xiro (close/tie, also spelled xidho).
- Irregular: kaalay / kaalaya (come), imow / imaada (come), dheh / dhaha (say), ahow / ahaada (be), orod / orda (run).
Negative imperative (prohibitive): ha + negative verb form (-in), plural adds -a: ha keenin / ha keenina, ha cunin / ha cunina, ha samayn, ha iman, ha oran. "Ha walwalin" (Don't worry). "Ha ilaawin" (Don't forget). "Ha ka baqin" (Don't be afraid of it).
Polite requests:
- Fadlan + imperative: "Fadlan ii sheeg" (Please tell me), "Fadlan ku celi" (Please repeat), "Fadlan tartiib u hadal" (Please speak slowly).
- Softer question forms: "Ma ii keeni kartaa...?" (Could you bring me...?), "Ma i caawin kartaa?" (Can you help me?). kar (can) + infinitive is the most natural polite request.
- "Bal" (just, go on) softens: "Bal i tus" (Show me, would you).
Third-person command / wish (optative): ha + subjunctive (-o): "Ha yimaado" (Let him come), "Ilaahay ha ku barakeeyo" (May God bless you), "Ilaahay ha u naxariisto" (May God have mercy on him/her). Negative wish: yaan / yuusan / yaanay: "Yuusan iman" (Let him not come), "Yaanay dhicin" (May it not happen).
First-person 'let me / let's': aan / aynu + subjunctive: "Aan arko" (Let me see), "Aan tagno" or "Aynu tagno" (Let's go), "Aynu bilowno" (Let's begin). Negative: "Yaynaan..." / "Aynaan" (let's not): "Aynaan dib u dhicin" (Let's not be late) – mostly written; in speech people say "Ha dib u dhicin" to the listener.
Directional particles combine with imperatives: soo (toward speaker) "Soo dhawoow" (welcome/come closer), "Soo gal" (come in), "Soo celi" (bring back); sii (onward) "Sii soco" (go on).
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/naxwe/08-hogatuska-baradigmaha-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Negation / Diidmada: ma, ha, aan, maya
knowledge.text:
Somali negation depends on clause type:
- Statements: ma before the verb, and the verb changes to a special negative form.
- Commands: ha + negative form (ha cunin = don't eat).
- Wishes: yaan / yuusan / yaanay (yuusan cunin = may he not eat).
- Inside relative and subordinate clauses: aan ("nin aan wax ogayn" = a man who does not know anything).
Negative paradigm, verb cun (eat):
| Present habitual: ma cuno (I/he), ma cuntid (you), ma cunto (she), ma cunno (we), ma cuntaan (you pl), ma cunaan (they) |
| Present progressive: ma cunayo (I/he), ma cunaysid (you), ma cunayso (she), ma cunayno (we), ma cunaysaan, ma cunayaan |
| Simple past: ma cunin – the SAME for every person ("Ma cunin" = I/you/he/she/we/they didn't eat) |
| Past habitual: ma cuni jirin | Future: ma cuni doono (doontid, doonto, doonno...) | Conditional: ma cuni lahayn |
The negative particle fuses with subject clitics: maan (ma + aan: "Maan fahmin" I didn't understand), muu ("Muu iman" he didn't come), may ("May tegin" she/they didn't go). "To be": ma ihi (I'm not), ma ihid (you aren't), ma aha (he/she/it isn't), ma ihin (we aren't), ma ahayn (wasn't). "Taasi ma aha" (That's not it). Adjective-verbs: "ma fiicna" (not good), "ma wanaagsana", "ma badna" (not much) – the negative adjective drops the fused 'be'.
Useful negative words:
- maya = no (answer). haa / haye = yes (haye is typical Northern).
- weli … ma = not yet: "Weli ma iman" (He hasn't come yet).
- weligay … ma = never (in my life): "Weligay ma arag" (I've never seen it). Also weligaa (you ever), weligiis (he ever).
- marna = never/not once; waxba = nothing ("Waxba ma haysto" I have nothing); cidna / qofna = nobody ("Cidna ma joogto" nobody is there); meelna = nowhere.
- "Dhib ma leh" = no problem; "Waxba ma aha" = it's nothing / never mind.
Negative questions: interrogative ma and negative ma must not be doubled (*"Axmed ma ma imanayo?" is wrong). Use focus: "Ma Axmed baan iman?" (Is it Axmed who didn't come?) or "Axmed miyaanu imanayn?" (Isn't Axmed coming?). Tag question: "... sow ma aha?" (... isn't it?).
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/naxwe/08-hogatuska-baradigmaha-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Questions and question words / Su'aalaha
knowledge.text:
Yes/no questions put ma (or miyaa / mi-) before the verb or with a focused element:
- "Ma timid?" (Did you come?) "Ma fahantay?" / "Miyaad fahantay?" (Did you understand?) "Ma nabad baa?" (Is it peace? = How are you?)
- "Shaah ma rabtaa?" (Do you want tea?) "Ma Cali baa?" (Is it Ali?)
- Choice questions use mise (or): "Shaah mise qaxwo?" (Tea or coffee?) – in statements 'or' is ama.
Question words (wh-words usually take a focus marker or fuse with clitics):
| maxaa / maxay / muxuu (what) | "Maxaad rabtaa?" What do you want? "Muxuu yiri?" What did he say? |
| yaa (who, as focused subject) / kuma, ayo (who) | "Yaa yimid?" Who came? "Waa kuma?" / "Waa ayo?" Who is it? |
| xaggee / halkee (where) | "Xaggee ayaad ka timid?" Where are you from? "Musqusha aawey?" Where is the toilet? (aawey = where is) |
| goorma / goormaa (when) | "Goormaad timaaddaa?" When are you coming? |
| sidee / sideed (how) | "Sidee tahay?" How are you? "Sidee loo sameeyaa?" How is it done? |
| immisa / imisa (how many / how much) | "Waa immisa?" How much is it? "Immisa jir baad tahay?" How old are you? |
| meeqa (how much, common in the South) | "Meeqa waaye?" How much is it? |
| kee / tee (which; suffixed: -kee m., -tee f.) | "Gurigee?" Which house? "Gabadhee?" Which girl? |
| maxaa … u / waayo (why) | "Maxaad u timid?" Why did you come? "Waayo?" Why? |
| maxaa yeelay / waayo (because) | "Ma iman karo, maxaa yeelay waan xanuunsanahay." |
Indirect questions use in / haddii: "Ma ogtahay inuu imanayo?" (Do you know whether he's coming?). "Ii sheeg goorta uu imanayo" (Tell me when he's coming).
Answers: "Haa" (yes), "Haye" (yes/OK, Northern), "Maya" (no), "Waa hagaag" / "Hagaag" (OK, fine), "Malaha" (maybe), "Insha Allah" (God willing – very common to answer future questions). Assistant tip: a recogniser may drop the initial ma; if a transcript reads like a statement but the user's intonation or context suggests a question ("Shaah rabtaa"), treat it as a question.
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Nouns, gender and definite articles / Magacyada iyo qodobada
knowledge.text:
Somali has no separate word for 'the' or 'a': definiteness is a suffix. The base consonant is k (masculine) or t (feminine); its shape changes with the sound before it.
Masculine (k-article):
- -ka after most consonants: nin → ninka (the man), wiil → wiilka (the boy), geed → geedka (the tree), dukaan → dukaanka (the shop), baabuur → baabuurka (the car).
- -ga after g and after most vowels: buug → buugga (the book), guri → guriga (the house), kursi → kursiga (the chair), dugsi → dugsiga (the school).
- -ha for nouns ending in -e/-o that change the vowel to -a: aabbe → aabbaha (the father), ilmo → ilmaha (the child/children).
- -a (k disappears) after q, x, c, kh, h, ': suuq → suuqa (the market), magac → magaca (the name), dhagax → dhagaxa (the stone).
Feminine (t-article):
- -ta after most consonants: naag → naagta (the woman), lug → lugta (the leg).
- -da after vowels and after d, x, c, q, h, ', w, y: hooyo → hooyada (the mother), magaalo → magaalada (the city), shaqo → shaqada (the work), bad → badda (the sea).
- -sha after l: bil → bisha (the month/moon), il → isha (the eye).
- -dha after r (the r changes): gabar → gabadha (the girl).
The same k/t rules apply to all determiners:
| -kan / -tan = this: buuggan, gabadhan, magaaladan |
| -kaas / -taas = that: ninkaas, gabadhaas |
| -kii / -tii = the (known, previously mentioned, or past): ninkii, gabadhii, "shalay ninkii yimid" (the man who came yesterday) |
| -kee / -tee = which?: ninkee, magaaladee |
Subject (nominative) form: when a definite noun is the non-focused subject, final -a becomes -u: ninku, gabadhu, magaaladu: "Ninku wuu yimid" (The man came). A focused subject keeps -a: "Ninka baa yimid". Recognisers often confuse -ka/-ku/-kii; meaning differs (object vs subject vs 'that/the aforementioned').
Gender is lexical: many feminines end in -o (hooyo, magaalo, shaqo) and many masculines in -e (aabbe, odey/oday "elder"), but there is no full rule. Tone also marks gender: ínan (boy) vs inán (girl), not written. Vocative endings: -ow (masc.: "Calow!" Oh Ali), -ey/-eey (fem.: "Faadumeey!").
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Hassan, Deqa (2011). Somali Dialects in the United States: How Intelligible is Af-Maay to Speakers of Af-Maxaa? MA thesis, Minnesota State Univ. https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/etds/276/

knowledge.title: Plurals and gender polarity / Wadarta
knowledge.text:
Somali plural formation is partly irregular, so learn plurals with the noun. Main patterns:
1. Short masculine nouns repeat the last consonant + -a-: buug → buugag (books), wiil → wiilal (boys), af → afaf (languages/mouths), dab → dabab (fires). nin → niman (men) is a common irregular member. 2. Feminine nouns ending in a consonant add -o: naag → naago (women), lug → lugo (legs), bil → bilo (months), gabar → gabdho (girls; vowel drops). 3. Many longer masculine nouns ending in a consonant add -o (often with a sound change): dukaan → dukaamo (shops), gacan → gacmo (hands, feminine noun), baabuur → baabuurro (cars), qalin → qalammo (pens). 4. Nouns ending in a vowel add -yaal or -ooyin: aabbe → aabbayaal (fathers), hooyo → hooyooyin (mothers), magaalo → magaalooyin (cities), guri → guryo (houses, irregular). 5. Arabic-style and irregular plurals: macallin → macallimiin (teachers), kursi → kuraas (chairs), il → indho (eyes), ilig → ilko (teeth), dhagax → dhagxan (stones). 6. Collectives used as plurals: dad (people), carruur (children), xoolo (livestock), biyo (water, grammatically plural: "biyaha" the water, "biyo badan" a lot of water).
Gender polarity: many nouns switch gender in the plural, which changes the article. buugga (the book, m.) → buugagta (the books, f.); naagta (the woman, f.) → naagaha (the women, m.); gabadha (the girl, f.) → gabdhaha (the girls, m.); hooyada → hooyooyinka.
Counting: after a number the noun usually stays in a special singular/genitive form: "laba buug" (two books), "saddex nin" (three men), "shan sano" (five years), "toban maalmood" (ten days), "afar saacadood" (four hours), "saddex bilood" (three months). Do not pluralise after numbers as in English (*"laba buugag").
Adjectives form plurals by repeating the first syllable: yar → yaryar (small), weyn → waaweyn (big), dheer → dhaadheer (tall/long), gaaban → gaagaaban (short): "carruur yaryar" (small children), "dhismayaal waaweyn" (big buildings).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Possessives: my, your, his... / Lahaanshaha
knowledge.text:
Possession is a suffix on the noun, built on the same k (masculine) / t (feminine) consonant as the definite article and following the same sound changes.
| Owner | masculine noun | feminine noun | example m. | example f. |
| my | -kayga | -tayda | buuggayga (my book) | gabadhayda (my daughter/girl) |
| your (sg) | -kaaga | -taada | gurigaaga (your house) | magaaladaada (your city) |
| his | -kiisa | -tiisa | magaciisa (his name) | hooyadiis (his mother) |
| her | -keeda | -teeda | aabbaheed (her father) | shaqadeeda (her work) |
| our (excl.) | -kayaga | -tayada | gurigayaga | magaaladayada |
| our (incl.) | -keenna | -teenna | dalkeenna (our country) | luuqaddeenna (our language) |
| your (pl) | -kiinna | -tiinna | gurigiinna | |
| their | -kooda | -tooda | magacooda | hooyadood |
Short forms (very common, especially with kinship and in speech): aabbahay (my father), hooyaday (my mother), walaalkay (my brother), walaashay (my sister), magacay (my name), "Magacaa?" (Your name? – short for magacaagu). Spelling variants: -kayga / -keyga, hooyaday / hooyadey.
Subject form ends in -u: "Magacaygu waa Cali" (My name is Ali). "Walaashay way imanaysaa" (My sister is coming).
'Of' constructions: possessor follows the possessed noun with genitive form: "guriga Cali" (Ali's house), "magaalada Muqdisho" (the city of Mogadishu), "hooyada carruurta" (the children's mother). With pronoun reference: "Cali gurigiisa" (Ali's house, lit. Ali his-house) is common in speech.
Assistant tips: (1) the owner's gender picks kiisa/keeda; the noun's gender picks k/t: "aabbaheed" (her father: masc noun, fem owner), "hooyadiis" (his mother: fem noun, masc owner). (2) Never attach English-style "my" as a separate word (*"anigaa buug").
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Adjectives, linking with 'oo' and gender agreement / Tilmaamaha iyo waafaqsanaanta
knowledge.text:
Adjectives follow the noun and do not themselves inflect for gender: "nin dheer" (a tall man), "gabar dheer" (a tall girl), "guri weyn" (a big house). The article goes on the noun: "ninka dheer" (the tall man).
Linking: two or more modifiers are joined with oo (and/which), and a predicate-like adjective often takes ah ('being'): "nin dheer oo caato ah" (a tall thin man), "magaalo qurux badan oo nabad ah" (a beautiful, peaceful city). Possessive/other modifiers linked with ee: "dukaanka dharka ee Cali" (Ali's clothes shop) – SLS treats the missing ee here as an error.
As predicates, adjectives fuse with 'to be' and agree with the subject: "Waan fiicanahay" (I am fine), "Waad fiicantahay" (you are fine), "Wuu fiican yahay" (he is fine), "Way fiican tahay" (she is fine), "Waan fiicannahay" (we are fine), "Waad fiicantihiin" (you pl are fine), "Way fiican yihiin" (they are fine). Example adjective-verb table (adag 'hard'): adkahay, adagtahay, adagyahay, adagtahay, adagnahay, adagtihiin, adagyihiin; negative: ma adka (it isn't hard).
Gender agreement on verbs: a feminine subject (grammatical gender, not natural sex) takes the -t- form in the 3rd person: "Asli baa keentay" (correct) vs *"Asli baa keenay". "Deeradu biyo bay cabtay" (The gazelle drank water) – deero is feminine, so bay/cabtay. Countries, cities and many abstract nouns are feminine: "Soomaaliya way horumartay", "Muqdisho waa magaalo weyn".
Common adjectives: wanaagsan (good), fiican (fine/good), xun (bad), weyn (big), yar (small), dheer (long/tall), gaaban (short), cusub (new), duug ah / hore (old, of things), qadiim (ancient), qurux badan (beautiful), kulul (hot), qabow (cold), macaan (sweet/delicious), qaali (expensive), jaban (cheap), dhow (near), fog (far), adag (hard), fudud (easy/light), culus (heavy), badan (many), yar (few). Comparison uses ka ... (more than): "Cali Axmed buu ka dheer yahay" (Ali is taller than Ahmed); superlative ugu: "Kan ugu weyn" (the biggest one).
Sources: https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/spec/grammar/0017-common-mistakes.md (CC BY 4.0); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Prepositional clitics u, ku, ka, la and their combinations / Meeleeyayaasha
knowledge.text:
Somali has four core prepositions, placed BEFORE the verb (not before the noun):
- u = to, for, towards: "Hooyo u dir" (send it to mother), "Maxaad u timid?" (why did you come? lit. for-what).
- ku = in, on, at, with (instrument): "Guriga ku jooga" (stay at home), "Qalin ku qor" (write with a pen).
- ka = from, about, than, out of: "Xamar ka imid" (came from Mogadishu), "Iga warran" (tell me about it), "Ka dheer" (taller than).
- la = with (accompaniment): "Ila kaalay" (come with me), "La hadal" (talk with).
They fuse with object pronouns:
| | i (me) | ku (you sg) | na (us excl.) | ina (us incl.) | idin (you pl) | la (impersonal) | is (self/each other) |
| u | ii | kuu | noo | inoo | idiin | loo | isu |
| ku | igu | kugu | nagu | inagu | idinku | lagu | isku |
| ka | iga | kaa | naga | inaga | idinka | laga | iska |
| la | ila | kula | nala | inala | idinla | lala | isla |
And two prepositions combine: u+ku = ugu, u+ka = uga, ku+ku / ku+ka / ka+ka = kaga, ku+la = kula, ka+la = kala. With pronouns these give forms like iigu, iiga, kuugu, kuuga, noogu, nooga, loogu, looga, igaga, lagaga, isugu, iskaga.
Everyday examples:
- "Biyo ii keen" (bring me water). "Ii sheeg" (tell me). "Kuu sheegi doonaa" (I'll tell you).
- "Iga raalli ahow" (forgive me / excuse me). "Waan kaa xumahay" (I'm sorry towards you). "Ka warran?" (what about...?).
- "Lacagta iigu soo dir EVC-ga" (send me the money through EVC). "Sawirka iigu dir WhatsApp" (send me the photo on WhatsApp).
- "Waxaa loogu yeeraa Dheere" (he is called Dheere). "Halkan waa laga gudbaa" (one crosses here).
- "Isku day" (try – lit. aim at self). "Iska warran" (how are you – lit. tell about yourself). "Iska jir!" (Be careful!). "Isla markiiba" (at once).
- "Ila soco" (walk with me). "Waan kula hadli doonaa" (I'll talk with you).
Order inside the verb group: [object pronoun] + [preposition(s)] + [directional soo/sii, adverbial wada/kala] + verb: "Ii soo dir" (send it to me), "Noo wada keena" (bring it all to us), "Kala qaado" (separate them). Many verbs have a fixed preposition: fariiso ku (sit on), dhaqaaq (move), ka bax (exit from), u baahan (need), ku faraxsan (happy with). SLS marks omission in such reviewed pairs as an error: "Mire baa ku fariistay kursiga" (correct) vs *"Mire baa fariistay kursiga".
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Conditionals, time clauses and 'would' / Shardiga
knowledge.text:
Real conditions use haddii (if) + subordinate verb (no focus particle, often -o subjunctive endings in the present). haddii fuses with subject clitics: haddaan (if I), haddaad (if you), hadduu (if he), haddii ay / hadday (if she/they), haddaynu (if we incl.).
- "Haddaad timaaddo, waan ku sugayaa" (If you come, I'll wait for you).
- "Hadduu roob da'o, ma imaan doono" (If it rains, he won't come).
- "Haddii Ilaahay idmo" / "Insha Allah" (if God permits) – used for almost any future plan.
- "Haddii kale" = otherwise: "Dhaqso, haddii kale waa nalaga tagayaa" (Hurry, otherwise we'll be left behind).
Unreal / counterfactual conditions use the infinitive + lahaa ('would'):
- "Haddaan lacag haysan lahaa, gaari baan iibsan lahaa" (If I had money, I would buy a car).
- "Haddaad ii sheegi lahayd, waan imaan lahaa" (If you had told me, I would have come).
- Negative: "ma iman lahayn" (would not have come).
Polite wish: "Waxaan jeclaan lahaa..." (I would like...).
Time and purpose clauses:
- marka / markaad / markuu = when: "Markaad gaarto ii soo wac" (When you arrive, call me).
- inta = while / as long as: "Inta aan sugayo" (while I wait). "Intaadan falin ka fiirso" (Before you act, look – proverb).
- kahor / ka hor = before; kadib / ka dib = after: "Cuntada ka dib" (after the meal), "Intaanan tegin" (before I go).
- si … u = in order to / so that: "Si aan u fahmo, tartiib u hadal" (Speak slowly so I can understand).
- in / inay / inuu = that (complement): "Waxaan rabaa inaan nasto" (I want to rest). "Waa inaad timaaddaa" (You must come – lit. it is that you come).
- in kasta oo = although: "In kasta oo uu daallan yahay, wuu shaqeeyay" (Although he was tired, he worked).
- sababtoo ah / maxaa yeelay / waayo = because; sidaas darteed = therefore.
Modal kar (can) + infinitive: "Waan sameyn karaa" (I can do it), "Ma iman karo" (I can't come), "Ma ii sheegi kartaa?" (Can you tell me?).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard/blob/main/resources/sarfe/02-falalka.md (CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Linking words and sentence connectors / Xiriiriyeyaasha
knowledge.text:
Somali distinguishes several words for 'and':
- iyo joins nouns/noun phrases: "shaah iyo rooti" (tea and bread), "Cali iyo Faadumo".
- oo joins clauses or verbs and links descriptive modifiers: "Wuu yimid oo wuu fadhiistay" (He came and sat down); "nin dheer oo caato ah".
- -na (suffix) = and/also on the second clause's first word: "Cali wuu yimid, Faadumana way timid" (Ali came, and Faadumo came). Also "Adna?" (And you?) in greetings.
- ee links clauses with a contrast or a relative after a definite head: "Ma aha Cali ee waa Axmed" (It's not Ali but Ahmed). "Waxa aad sheegtay ee ah..." (what you said, which is...).
Other connectors:
| laakiin / se / -se = but ("Waan rabaa, laakiin lacag ma haysto") |
| ama = or (statements); mise = or (questions) |
| haddana = and yet, then again; mar kale = again |
| sidoo kale = also, likewise | xitaa = even |
| markaa / markaas = then, so | kadib = afterwards | ugu horrayn = first of all | ugu dambayn = finally |
| tusaale ahaan = for example | taas macnaheedu waa = that means |
| sababtoo ah / maxaa yeelay / waayo = because | sidaas darteed = therefore |
| haddii / haddii kale = if / otherwise | inkasta oo = although |
| intaa waxaa dheer = in addition | si kastaba ha ahaatee = in any case, anyway |
Discourse words common in speech: "Waar" (hey, man – addressing a male), "Naa" (hey – addressing a female, can sound rude/familiar), "Walaal" (brother/sister, neutral polite address), "Haye" (OK), "Hagaag" (fine), "Waa yahay" (alright, agreed), "Bal" (just, let's see), "Ee" (well...), "Sax" (correct), "Haa, waa sidaas" (yes, that's right), "Sidee?" (how so?).
Assistant tip: in conversational output prefer short clauses joined by oo and -na rather than long English-style sentences. "Waan ku caawin karaa, waxaanse u baahanahay magacaaga" (I can help you, but I need your name).
Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_grammar; https://github.com/goobolabs/somali-language-standard (Somali Language Standard, CC BY 4.0); Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Greetings and replies / Salaanta iyo jawaabaha
knowledge.text:
Islamic greeting (used everywhere, by phone too):
- "Assalaamu calaykum" (peace be upon you) → reply "Wacalaykumu salaam" (and upon you peace). Somali spelling uses c for the Arabic ʿayn: calaykum. Fuller reply: "Wacalaykumu salaam wa raxmatullaahi wa barakaatuh".
Everyday greetings:
- "Iska warran?" (How are you? lit. tell about yourself) → "Waan fiicanahay" / "Nabad" / "Alxamdulillaah, waan iska fiicanahay" (Praise God, I'm fine). Plural: "Iska warrama?"
- "Ma nabad baa?" (Is all well? lit. is it peace?) → "Waa nabad" / "Nabad weeye" / "Nabad waaye".
- "Sidee tahay?" / "Side tahay?" / Southern "Seetahay?" (How are you?) → "Waan fiicanahay, adiguna?" (I'm fine, and you?) / "Adna?"
- "Ii warran" / "Bal ka warran" (What's new? tell me news). "Maxaa cusub?" (What's new?)
- "Maxaad sheegtay?" (What's new? lit. what did you tell) – friendly, common in the north.
Time-of-day: "Subax wanaagsan" (good morning), "Galab wanaagsan" (good afternoon), "Fiid wanaagsan" (good evening), "Habeen wanaagsan" (good night), "Maalin wanaagsan" (have a good day). Welcome: "Soo dhawoow" (welcome, to a male; also written soo dhowow), "Soo dhawaaw" (to a female), "Soo dhawaada" (plural). Reply: "Mahadsanid" / "Ku soo dhawoow adiguna". Meeting someone: "Magacaa?" / "Magacaagu waa maxay?" (What's your name?) → "Magacaygu waa Cali" / "Waxaa la i yiraahdaa Cali" (I'm called Ali). "Barasho wanaagsan" (nice to meet you). "Xaggee ayaad ka timid?" → "Waxaan ka imid Hargeysa." Long time no see: "Wakhti dheer kuma arag" / "Muddo dheer kuma arag" (I haven't seen you for a long time). Partings: "Nabadgelyo" (goodbye, lit. go in peace; reply also "Nabadgelyo"), "Nabadeey", "Is arag dambe" (see you later), "Berri is aragno" (see you tomorrow), "Ilaahay ha kuu sahlo" (may God make it easy for you), "Ilaa goor dambe" (until later). Etiquette: greet before any request; with elders use full salaam and "adeer" / "abti" / "eeddo" / "habaryar" or "hooyo" / "aabbo" as respectful address. Greeting exchanges often repeat "nabad" and "alxamdulillaah" several times; an assistant should reply in kind before getting to business, but briefly.
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; https://wikitravel.org/en/Somali_phrasebook; Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Politeness, thanks, apologies and forms of address / Edebta, mahadnaqa iyo raalli-gelinta
knowledge.text:
Please and thanks:
- "Fadlan" (please) – placed first: "Fadlan i sug" (please wait for me).
- "Mahadsanid" (thank you, sg); "Mahadsanidiin" (to several people); "Aad baad u mahadsantahay" / "Aad iyo aad baad u mahadsan tahay" (thank you very much); "Waad mahadsantahay".
- Religious thanks: "Ilaahay ha ku abaal mariyo" (may God reward you), "Jazaakallaahu khayran" (Arabic, same meaning).
- Reply to thanks: "Adaa mudan" / "Adigaa mudan" (you deserve [the thanks]), "Waxba ma aha" (it's nothing), "Dhib ma leh" (no problem).
Apologies:
- "Waan ka xumahay" (I'm sorry; lit. I feel bad about it). "Aad baan uga xumahay" (I'm very sorry).
- "Iga raalli ahow" (forgive me / excuse me; to a group "iga raalli ahaada"). Spelled raalli or raali in practice.
- "Cudurdaar" (an excuse, a formal apology).
- "Ma ula jeedin" (I didn't mean it). "Khalad baa dhacay" (a mistake happened).
- Accepting: "Dhib ma leh", "Waan kaa raalli ahay" (I forgive you / I'm fine with you), "Waa hagaag".
Forms of address (kinship terms are used as respectful titles for non-relatives):
| aabbo / aabbe – father; respectful to an older man | hooyo – mother; respectful/affectionate to an older woman, also used by mothers to children |
| adeer – paternal uncle; polite to an older man | abti – maternal uncle; friendly-respectful to a man |
| eeddo – paternal aunt | habaryar – maternal aunt (lit. little mother) |
| walaal – brother/sister; the neutral polite "friend" for peers and strangers | ina'adeer – cousin (paternal uncle's child) |
| awoowe – grandfather | ayeeyo – grandmother |
| Mudane – Mr./Sir (formal) | Marwo – Mrs./Madam (formal); Marwada = the lady |
| Sheekh – religious teacher/scholar | Macallin / Macallimad – teacher (m/f), also respectful |
| Ustaad – teacher, lecturer | Dhakhtar – doctor (also as a title: Dhakhtar Cali) |
Register tips for an assistant: default to "walaal" or the user's name; avoid "naa" and bare "waar" with strangers (too familiar). Use "fadlan" with requests and "mahadsanid" after help. Older users often appreciate du'a-style closings ("Ilaahay ha kuu fududeeyo" – may God make it easy for you).
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf

knowledge.title: Condolences, illness and hard news / Tacsi iyo booqashada bukaanka
knowledge.text:
Death and condolence (tacsi). Somali condolence language is religious and formulaic; using the right phrase matters more than originality.
- On hearing of a death: "Innaa lillaahi wa innaa ilayhi raajicuun" (Qur'an 2:156: "To God we belong and to Him we return").
- For the deceased: "Ilaahay ha u naxariisto" (May God have mercy on him/her). Variant: "Allaha u naxariisto". Plural deceased: "Ilaahay ha u naxariisto dhammaantood".
- For the family: "Ilaahay samir iyo iimaan ha idin siiyo" (May God give you patience and faith). To one person: "Ilaahay samir ha ku siiyo".
- "Ilaahay jannadii ha ka waraabiyo" (May God give him/her drink from Paradise) is also widely heard.
- Words: geeri (death), dhimasho (dying, death), aas (burial/funeral), tacsi (condolence visit), baroor (mourning, wailing), duco (prayer), qabri (grave), kafan (shroud).
- Polite verbs: "Wuu geeriyooday" / "Way geeriyootay" (he/she passed away) are gentler than "wuu dhintay" (he died).
- Funerals happen quickly (often the same day), so an assistant should not suggest scheduling days ahead; offer practical help (contacts, directions to the mosque/cemetery, sending condolence messages).
Illness:
- "Ilaahay ha ku caafiyo" (May God heal you) / to a third person "Ilaahay ha caafiyo". "Caafimaad Ilaahay ha ku siiyo".
- "Caafimaad ayaan kuu rajaynayaa" (I wish you good health / get well soon).
- "Iska jir" (take care), "Nasasho qaado" (get some rest).
- Asking: "Sidee tahay maanta?" (How are you today?), "Maxaa ku xanuunaya?" (What hurts?), "Ma ka roonaatay?" (Are you feeling better?).
Other hard news: "Ilaahay ha kuu sahlo" (May God make it easy for you), "Samir" (patience), "Ilaahay baa mahad leh" (praise be to God – said even in difficulty), "Qadar Ilaahay" (God's decree). Assistant rule of thumb: answer condolence messages with one of the fixed phrases above plus a short, sincere line; do not use jokes, emojis or English idioms like "sorry for your loss" translated literally.
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Congratulations, weddings, Eid and Ramadan wishes / Hambalyo, aroos, ciid iyo Ramadaan
knowledge.text:
Congratulations:
- "Hambalyo!" (Congratulations!) – the general word: "Hambalyo, shaqada cusub!" (Congrats on the new job). "Hambalyo ku saabsan..." (congratulations on...).
- "Mabruuk!" (Arabic, very common for weddings, births, new homes, cars). Reply: "Allaha kugu barakeeyo" / "Ilaahay kuu barakeeyo" (God bless you too).
- "Guul ayaan kuu rajaynayaa" (I wish you success – before exams, travel, business).
- "Dhalasho wanaagsan" (happy birthday) – used, though birthdays are less central in traditional culture.
- New baby: "Mabruuk, Ilaahay ha idiin barakeeyo ilmaha" (Congratulations, may God bless the child for you).
Weddings (aroos):
- Vocabulary: aroos (wedding/wedding party), meher (Islamic marriage contract, nikah), yarad (bride wealth given to the bride's family), aqal-gal (the couple's entering their home), shaash-saar (ceremony a few days after the wedding when the bride is given the married woman's headscarf).
- Wishes: "Mabruuk!", "Ilaahay ha idiin barakeeyo" (May God bless it for you both), the Prophetic wedding du'a "Baarakallaahu lakumaa wa baaraka calaykumaa wa jamaca baynakumaa fii khayr".
Eid (ciid):
- Ciidul Fidri / Ciidda Soonfurka (Eid al-Fitr, end of Ramadan) and Ciidul Adxa / Ciid Carrafo (Eid al-Adha, during the pilgrimage month).
- Wishes: "Ciid wanaagsan!" (Happy Eid), "Ciid Mubaarak!", "Ciid saciid!", "Taqabbalallaahu minnaa wa minkum" (May God accept from us and from you). Reply with the same.
- Ciidda Carrafo is the 10th of the lunar month Arrafo/Carrafo (Dhul-Hijja), and "Maalinta Carrafo" (Day of Arafa) is the day before.
Ramadan (Ramadaan / Soon):
- "Ramadaan kariim" / "Ramadaan Mubaarak" (blessed Ramadan), "Soon wanaagsan" (good fasting).
- soon (fasting), afur (the evening meal that breaks the fast; "Afurku waa saacaddee?" When is iftar?), suxuur (pre-dawn meal), taraawiix (night prayers), sako / sakada fidriga (zakat al-fitr), "Ilaahay ha naga aqbalo soonka" (May God accept our fast).
Assistant tip: during Ramadan avoid suggesting daytime meals or coffee meetings; times like "afurka kadib" (after iftar) are normal for plans.
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Kapchits, G. On the Somali Temporal Lexicon. Bildhaan vol. 19 (2019). https://digitalcommons.macalester.edu/bildhaan/vol19/iss1/7; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Phone-call phrases / Erayada wicitaanka taleefanka
knowledge.text:
Opening and identifying:
- "Haloo" / "Hallo" (Hello – answering the phone), then usually "Assalaamu calaykum".
- "Waa kuma?" (Who is it? – Northern) / "Waa ayo?" (Who is it? – common in the South). "Yaa ii soo wacay?" (Who called me?)
- "Waa aniga, Cali" / "Waxaa ku hadlaya Cali" (It's me, Ali / Ali speaking).
- "Ma Faadumo baa?" (Is that Faadumo?) "Faadumo ma joogtaa?" (Is Faadumo there?)
Connection problems:
- "Ma i maqlaysaa?" (Can you hear me?) → "Haa, waan ku maqlayaa" / "Si fiican kuma maqlayo" (I can't hear you well).
- "Codku wuu go'ayaa" (The sound keeps cutting out). "Khadka ayaa go'ay" (The line dropped). "Shabakad ma jirto" / "Network-ga ayaa xun" (No network / bad network).
- "Kor u qaad codka" (Speak louder). "Tartiib u hadal" (Speak slowly). "Ku celi fadlan" (Repeat, please).
- "Dib ii soo wac" (Call me back). "Waan kuu soo wici doonaa" (I'll call you). "Daqiiqad i sug" / "Sug yar" (Hold on a minute).
- "Hadda mashquul baan ahay" (I'm busy now). "Shir baan ku jiraa" (I'm in a meeting). "Baabuur baan wadayaa" (I'm driving).
Messages and numbers:
- "Fariin ii soo dir" (Send me a message), "Iigu soo dir WhatsApp-ka" (Send it to me on WhatsApp), "Codka ii soo dir" (Send me a voice note).
- "Lambarkaaga i sii" (Give me your number). "Lambarkaygu waa 61 ..." – numbers are read digit by digit or in pairs: "lix kow, toddoba labaatan..." Somali mobile numbers are often grouped in twos/threes; confirm by reading back.
- "Lacagta iigu soo dir EVC-ga" (Send me the money via EVC). "Ma heshay?" (Did you get it?) "Waan helay, mahadsanid."
Closing: "Hagaag, nabadgelyo" (OK, goodbye), "Is arag dambe", "Ilaahay kuu sahlo". Somalis often close with mutual du'a. Assistant/voice tips: callers often begin with salaam and a long greeting; do not interrupt it. If the line is poor, ask "Ma i maqlaysaa?" and confirm key facts (names, numbers, amounts) by repeating them back.
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf

knowledge.title: Asking for and giving directions, transport / Jihooyinka iyo gaadiidka
knowledge.text:
Asking:
- "Isbitaalku xaggee buu ku yaal?" (Where is the hospital?); short form "... aawey?": "Masjidka aawey?" (Where's the mosque?)
- "Sideen ku gaaraa suuqa?" (How do I get to the market?)
- "Meeshani waa xagee?" (Where is this place?) "Ma dhow yahay mise wuu fog yahay?" (Is it near or far?)
- "Immisa daqiiqo ayay ku qaadanaysaa?" (How many minutes does it take?)
Giving directions:
- "Toos u soco" (go straight), "Midig u leexo" (turn right), "Bidix u leexo" (turn left), "Dib u noqo" (go back), "Ka gudub waddada" (cross the road).
- "Isgoyska ku leexo" (turn at the junction), "Wareegga" (the roundabout), "Waddada weyn / laamiga" (the main/tarmac road), "Luuqda" (the alley/lane).
- Position words (with possessive): "agtiisa" (near it), "hortiisa" (in front of it), "gadaashiisa" (behind it), "dhinaciisa" (beside it), "ka soo horjeeda" (opposite), "dhexda" (in the middle), "ka hor" (before), "ka dib" (after), "korka" (on top/upstairs), "hoosta" (below/downstairs).
- Distance: "Way dhow tahay" (it's near), "Way fog tahay" (it's far), "Waa laba tallaabo" (it's a couple of steps), "Waa toban daqiiqo oo lugeyn ah" (ten minutes' walk).
- Directions of the compass: waqooyi (north), koonfur (south), bari (east), galbeed (west).
Transport:
- baabuur / gaari (car), bas (bus), bajaaj (three-wheeler taxi, very common in Somali cities), tagsi / taksi (taxi), mooto (motorbike), diyaarad (aeroplane), garoon diyaaradeed / garoonka (airport), markab (ship), dekad (port).
- "Halkan i dhig" (drop me here), "Joogso halkan" (stop here), "Immisa ayaad ku qaadaysaa?" (How much do you charge?), "Ii qaad suuqa" (take me to the market).
- Local landmarks dominate directions in Somali cities more than street names; an assistant should ask for or offer a nearby landmark (masjid, hotel, market, KM4 junction in Mogadishu, etc.) instead of only a street address.
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf

knowledge.title: Shopping and bargaining / Iibsiga iyo gorgortanka
knowledge.text:
Asking prices:
- "Waa immisa?" / "Waa imisa?" (How much is it?) – standard. "Meeqa waaye?" / "Meeqa?" (How much? – common in the South/Mogadishu). "Qiimihiisu waa immisa?" (What's its price?)
- "Kiiladu waa immisa?" (How much per kilo?) "Mid kasta waa immisa?" (How much each?)
- Answer: "Waa konton shilin" (It's 50 shillings), "Waa shan doollar" (It's five dollars), "Toban kun oo shilin" (10,000 shillings).
Bargaining (gorgortan):
- "Waa qaali!" (It's expensive!) "Aad bay qaali u tahay" (It's very expensive).
- "Wax iga dhim" (Reduce it for me / give me a discount). "Qiimo dhimis ma jiraa?" (Is there a discount?)
- "Ugu dambayn waa immisa?" (What's your last price?) "Intaas ka hoos ma jiro?" (Nothing below that?)
- "Saddex doollar ayaan ku siinayaa" (I'll give you three dollars). "Waa hagaag, keen" (OK, give it).
- Seller: "Waa qiimihiisa" (That's its price), "Qiimo go'an" (fixed price), "Waa jaban yahay" (it's cheap), "Tayo fiican" (good quality).
Buying:
- "Ma haysaa ...?" (Do you have ...?) "Waxaan rabaa laba kiilo oo bariis ah" (I want two kilos of rice).
- "Waan qaadanayaa" (I'll take it). "I tus kan" (Show me this one). "Mid kale ma jiraa?" (Is there another one?) "Cabbir weyn/yar" (bigger/smaller size).
- Payment: "Lacag caddaan ah" (cash), "EVC ku bixi" / "Zaad ku bixi" (pay by mobile money), "Baaqiga i sii" (give me the change), "Rasiid ii sii" (give me a receipt), "Dayn ii qor" (put it on my tab – credit in local shops).
- Containers/units: bac (plastic bag), kartoon (carton), kiilo, nus kiilo (half kilo), litir (litre), gaalan (jerrycan), xabbad (piece, one item: "laba xabbo" two pieces).
Common goods: bariis (rice), baasto (pasta), sonkor (sugar), bur (flour), saliid (cooking oil), caano (milk), shaah (tea), hilib (meat), digaag (chicken), kalluun (fish), khudaar (vegetables), miro (fruit), moos (banana), timir (dates), biyo (water), rooti (bread), canjeero (Somali pancake), sabuun (soap). Markets: Bakaaraha (Mogadishu's main market), Suuqa Waaheen (Hargeysa).
Sources: https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Numbers and counting / Tirada iyo tirinta
knowledge.text:
Cardinal numbers:
| 0 eber | 1 kow (hal before a noun) | 2 laba | 3 saddex | 4 afar | 5 shan | 6 lix | 7 toddoba | 8 siddeed | 9 sagaal | 10 toban |
| 11 kow iyo toban | 12 laba iyo toban | 13 saddex iyo toban ... 19 sagaal iyo toban |
| 20 labaatan | 30 soddon | 40 afartan | 50 konton | 60 lixdan | 70 toddobaatan | 80 siddeetan | 90 sagaashan |
| 100 boqol | 200 laba boqol | 1,000 kun | 2,000 laba kun | 10,000 toban kun | 100,000 boqol kun | 1,000,000 malyuun (also milyan, milyoon) | 1,000,000,000 bilyan |
Compounds: units come first, joined with iyo: 21 = kow iyo labaatan, 35 = shan iyo soddon, 99 = sagaal iyo sagaashan. Hundreds/thousands come first: 150 = boqol iyo konton, 1,250 = kun iyo laba boqol iyo konton, 2026 = laba kun iyo lix iyo labaatan. Spelling variants: toddoba/todoba, siddeed/sideed, soddon/soddan, labo (Southern) for laba.
Using numbers with nouns: "hal nin" (one man), "laba buug" (two books), "saddex gabdhood" (three girls), "toban sano" (ten years), "shan maalmood" (five days), "afar saacadood" (four hours). The noun is not made plural after a number.
Ordinals add -aad: koowaad / kowaad (1st), labaad (2nd), saddexaad (3rd), afraad (4th), shanaad (5th), tobnaad (10th), "bisha labaad" (the second month = February).
Fractions and quantities: badh / bar (half; "saddex iyo badh" = 3½), rubuc (quarter), saddex meelood meel (one third), boqolkiiba (percent: "boqolkiiba toban" = 10%), labanlaab (double), dhowr (several), qaar (some), dhammaan (all).
Dates: day number + -da: "kowda" (the 1st), "labada" (the 2nd), "saddexda bisha" (the 3rd of the month). "Taariikhdu waa immisa maanta?" (What's the date today?) Somali dates are written day/month/year. Ages: "Immisa jir baad tahay?" → "Waxaan ahay labaatan jir" (I'm 20 years old). Phone numbers: read digit by digit or in pairs; confirm by repeating.
Sources: https://wikitravel.org/en/Somali_phrasebook; https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php; Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words)

knowledge.title: Money and payments / Lacagta iyo lacag-bixinta
knowledge.text:
Currencies people talk about:
- Shilin Soomaali (Somali shilling, SOS) – in daily speech "shilin"; "kun" (a thousand-shilling note/unit) is used as shorthand for amounts.
- Shilinka Soomaaliland (Somaliland shilling) in Hargeysa and the north-west.
- Doollar (US dollar) – the main currency for larger prices across Somalia: "Waa toban doollar" (it's ten dollars). Cents: "sent" / "senti".
- Neighbouring: birr (Ethiopian birr – Somali Region of Ethiopia), shilinka Kenya (Kenyan shilling), faran / faranka Jabuuti (Djiboutian franc).
Mobile money (lacagta moobaylka) dominates payments in Somali territories. Brand names a recogniser must keep intact: EVC Plus (Hormuud, Somalia), ZAAD (Telesom, Somaliland), Sahal (Golis, Puntland), eDahab (Somtel). Typical phrases:
- "EVC ku soo dir" (send it via EVC), "Lacagta ma heshay?" (Did you get the money?), "Waan kuu diray" (I sent it to you), "Lambarka EVC-gaaga i sii" (give me your EVC number).
- "Haraaga" / "Baaqiga" (balance / remainder), "Kaarka" (airtime; "kaar ku shub" = load airtime).
Remittance: xawaalad (hawala money-transfer company; e.g., Dahabshiil, Amal, Taaj, Iftin), "lacag ayaa la ii soo diray" (money was sent to me), "Lacag-dirid" (sending money).
Vocabulary:
| lacag – money | lacag caddaan ah – cash | qiime / sicir – price, rate | kharash – expense, cost |
| mushahar – salary | dakhli – income | deyn / dayn – debt | amaah – loan, borrowing |
| bangi – bank | akoon / koonto – account | dhigasho – deposit | lacag la bixid / ka-bixid – withdrawal |
| sarrif – currency exchange | sarrifle – money changer | faa'iido – profit, interest | khasaare – loss |
| canshuur – tax | rasiid – receipt | biil – bill | ganacsi – business, trade |
| sako – zakat (alms) | sadaqo – charity | ribo – usury/interest (religiously prohibited) | maalgashi – investment |
Example: "Biishii korontada waxaan ku bixiyay EVC" (I paid the electricity bill via EVC). Local banks people name include Salaam Somali Bank and Premier Bank. Islamic finance terms (murabaxa, mudaraba) are common in bank talk.
Sources: Saeed, John I. (1999). Somali. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (condensed in own words); Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf; https://www.omniglot.com/language/phrases/somali.php

knowledge.title: Telling time: clock time vs. Somali time / Saacadda iyo wakhtiga
knowledge.text:
Asking: "Saacaddu waa immisa?" / "Waa immisa saacaddu?" / "Saacaddu waa meeqa?" / short "Waa immisadii?" (What time is it?) Answering: the hour number takes a definite ending -da/-ta or -dii/-tii: "Waa labadii" / "Saacaddu waa labada" (It's two o'clock). "Waa kowdii" (one o'clock), "saddexdii", "afartii", "shantii", "lixdii", "toddobadii", "siddeeddii", "sagaalkii", "tobankii", "kow iyo tobankii", "laba iyo tobankii".
- Half past: iyo badh / iyo bar: "Waa saddexdii iyo badh" (3:30).
- Quarter past: iyo rubuc: "Waa afartii iyo rubuc" (4:15).
- Quarter to: rubuc u dhiman: "Waa rubuc u dhiman saddexda" (2:45).
- Minutes: daqiiqo: "shantii iyo toban daqiiqo" (5:10). Seconds: ilbiriqsi.
- At (time): "Saddexda ayaan imanayaa" / "saacadda saddexaad" (at three).
Somali time (traditional reckoning). Many Somalis – especially in rural areas, among elders and in southern towns – count hours from sunrise (about 6:00), like Swahili time. The Somali hour = clock hour minus 6:
| 07:00 → kowdii subaxnimo (1 in the morning) | 09:00 → saddexdii subaxnimo | 12:00 → lixdii (6, midday) | 13:00 → toddobadii galabnimo | 18:00 → laba iyo tobankii (12, sunset) | 19:00 → kowdii habeennimo (1 at night) | 21:00 → saddexdii habeennimo |
Clocks and watches are still set to standard (international) time; context words decide which system is meant.
Parts of the day (used constantly instead of exact times; several tie to prayer times):
| waaberi / aroor – dawn | subax / subaxnimo – morning | barqo – late morning (about 9–11) | duhur – noon/early afternoon (Dhuhr prayer) |
| galab / galabnimo – afternoon | casar – late afternoon (Asr prayer) | maqrib / fiid – sunset, early evening | cisho / cishe – nightfall (Isha prayer, ~8 pm) |
| habeen / habeennimo – night | saqdhexe – midnight | caawa – tonight | xalay – last night | saaka – this morning | galabta – this afternoon |
Assistant rules for scheduling and voice: (1) When a user says a bare hour like "saacadda toban" or "tobanka subaxnimo", confirm which system if the result would be ambiguous: "Ma waxaad ula jeeddaa 10:00 subaxnimo (saacadda caalamka) mise 4:00 galabnimo (saacadda Soomaalida)?" (2) Prayer-anchored times ("casarka kadib", "maqribka kahor") are normal; convert them using local prayer times. (3) In East Africa Time (EAT, UTC+3) the sun rises around 6, so Somali time is reliable year-round.
Sources: http://hooyo.web.free.fr/E_chap32.html; https://www.luuqad.com/learn-somali/asking-questions/waa-immisa-saacaddu/; https://wikitravel.org/en/Somali_phrasebook; Iska wax u qabso: A Somali Language Learning Manual (Centro Studi Somali, Roma Tre) https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/bitstream/2307/5860/1/Iska%20wax%20u%20qabso_A%20Somali%20Language%20Learning%20Manual.pdf

knowledge.title: Days, months, seasons and relative dates / Maalmaha, bilaha iyo xilliyada
knowledge.text:
Days of the week (from Arabic; the Somali week traditionally starts on Saturday):
| Sabti – Saturday | Axad – Sunday | Isniin – Monday | Talaado (Salaasa) – Tuesday | Arbaco – Wednesday | Khamiis – Thursday | Jimce – Friday |
Definite forms: Sabtida, Axadda, Isniinta, Talaadada, Arbacada, Khamiista, Jimcaha. "Jimcaha" (Friday) is the weekly holiday in Somalia; many offices also close Thursday afternoon. Week = toddobaad (also usbuuc, wiig). Weekend = dhammaadka toddobaadka.
Relative days: maanta (today), berri (tomorrow), saadambe (the day after tomorrow), shalay (yesterday), dorraad (the day before yesterday). "Toddobaadkan" (this week), "toddobaadka dambe / soo socda" (next week), "toddobaadkii hore / la soo dhaafay" (last week), "bishan" (this month), "sannadkan" (this year), "sannadka dambe" (next year).
Gregorian months (loans from Italian/English; several spellings are in use):
Jannaayo, Febraayo, Maarso, Abriil, Maajo, Juun, Luulyo, Agoosto, Sebtembar (Sabtembar), Oktoobar, Nofembar (Noofembar), Diseembar. Formal/CLDR style uses ordinals: Bisha Koobaad (January), Bisha Labaad (February) ... Bisha Laba iyo Tobnaad (December). Month = bil / bisha (also 'moon'); year = sannad / sano.
Seasons (the Somali year has two rainy and two dry seasons):
| Jiilaal – the main dry season (about December–March), the hardest season for herders |
| Gu' – the main rainy season (about April–June); most important rains |
| Xagaa – the cooler dry season (about July–September), with coastal drizzle |
| Dayr – the short rainy season (about October–November) |
Wet seasons together are called Nur; Dabshid / Neyruus is the traditional solar new year festival (dab-shid = lighting fire), famous in Afgooye with the istun stick-fight. Abaar = drought; roob = rain; daad = flood.
Example sentences: "Isniinta soo socota ayaan kuu imanayaa" (I'm coming to you next Monday). "Bisha Maarso dhammaadkeeda" (at the end of March). "Gu'ga roobabkiisu way yaraadeen" (The Gu' rains were poor).
Sources: Kapchits, G. On the Somali Temporal Lexicon. Bildhaan vol. 19 (2019). https://digitalcommons.macalester.edu/bildhaan/vol19/iss1/7; http://hooyo.web.free.fr/E_chap33.html; https://wikitravel.org/en/Somali_phrasebook; https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/44/verify/dates/so.html

knowledge.title: Islamic months and the traditional Somali lunar calendar / Bilaha hijriga iyo magacyadooda Soomaaliga
knowledge.text:
Somalis use three calendars: the Gregorian (official/business), the Islamic Hijri lunar calendar (religious life, Ramadan, Eid), and a traditional solar calendar used by herders and farmers. The lunar months have Arabic names, but traditional Somali names are still widely understood, especially by elders and in rural areas.
Hijri month – traditional Somali name(s) (from G. Kapchits, "On the Somali Temporal Lexicon", Bildhaan 2019):
| 1 Muxarram – Dago, Seko/Sako |
| 2 Safar – Safar, Miira |
| 3 Rabiicul Awwal – Mawliid / Mowliid (the Prophet's birthday month) |
| 4 Rabiicul Aakhir – Maalmadoone |
| 5 Jamaadal Awwal – Rajal hore, Ban hore, Mille hore |
| 6 Jamaadal Aakhir – Rajal dhexe, Ban dambe, Mille dambe, Dabbooje |
| 7 Rajab – Rajal dambe, Sabbuux, Cawismaan |
| 8 Shacbaan – Waabberiis, Soondheere, Gasayr |
| 9 Ramadaan – Soon, Soonqaad |
| 10 Shawwaal – Soonfur |
| 11 Dul Qacda – Sidataal |
| 12 Dul Xijja – Arrafo / Carrafo, Xaj |
Other popular lists shift the middle names: e.g., Seko, Safar, Mawliid, Rajal hore, Rajal dhexe, Rajal dambe, Sabbuux (= Rajab), Waaberiis, Soon, Soonfur, Sidataal, Carrafo – i.e., Rajal hore/dhexe/dambe for months 4–6. When precision matters, give the Arabic month name too. Puglielli & Mansuur's dictionary defines arrafo (variant carrafo) as the last month of the Somali lunar year, in which the pilgrimage is performed.
Key dates in Somali usage:
- Ramadaan / Soon: month of fasting; "Soonfur" month begins with Ciidul Fidri (Eid al-Fitr).
- Maalinta Carrafo (Day of Arafa, 9 Dul Xijja) and Ciidul Adxa / Ciid Carrafo (10 Dul Xijja).
- Mawliid: celebration of the Prophet's birthday (12 Rabiicul Awwal), observed with religious gatherings in many Somali communities.
- Islamic new year: 1 Muxarram (bisha Dago).
Hijri dates shift about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year; exact days depend on moon sighting ("dayax arag"), so Somali authorities may announce Eid a day earlier or later than neighbouring countries. An assistant should give Hijri dates as approximate unless an official announcement is available.
Sources: Kapchits, G. On the Somali Temporal Lexicon. Bildhaan vol. 19 (2019). https://digitalcommons.macalester.edu/bildhaan/vol19/iss1/7; http://hooyo.web.free.fr/E_chap33.html; Puglielli, A. & Cabdalla Cumar Mansuur (2012). Qaamuuska Af-Soomaaliga. RomaTrE-Press https://romatrepress.uniroma3.it/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/qaam-cama.pdf; http://xikmadmaal.blogspot.com/2013/04/aqoonguud-maalmaha-iyo-afka-soomaaliga.html

knowledge.title: About Somali proverbs / Maahmaahda Soomaaliyeed
knowledge.text:
A maahmaah (plural maahmaahyo) is a fixed traditional saying. Proverbs are central to Somali speech: elders use them to settle disputes, poets weave them into verse, and ordinary speakers drop one into conversation to win an argument politely. The best-known proverb about proverbs is "Soomaali been ma maahmaahdo" (Somalis do not lie in proverbs; also recorded as "Soomaalidu been way sheegtaa, been kuma maahmaahdo" – Somalis may tell lies, but never in a proverb). It means a proverb carries accepted truth.
Related terms: murti (wisdom, wise saying), oraah / odhaah (saying, phrase), hal-hays (catchphrase, motto), sarbeeb (allusive figurative speech), googaaleysi (riddle game), suugaan (literature, oral and written).
Major collections: Georgi Kapchits compiled the Dictionary of Somali Proverbs (Qaamuuska Maahmaahyada Soomaaliyeed, Moscow 1988) and "Soomaali been ma maahmaahdo / Somalis do not lie in proverbs" (2012, 249 popular proverbs plus thousands more); Mohammed Sh. Hassan's "Diiwaanka Maahmaahyada" (1997) lists over 1,000. Many proverbs alliterate (repeat the first consonant: "Biyo sacabbadaada...", "Gar iyo geeri") and use pastoral images – camels (geel), water wells (ceel), milk (caano), drought (abaar), hyenas (dhurwaa).
How an assistant should use them: (1) quote only genuine proverbs (those in this library or verified collections) – never invent a saying in proverb form; (2) give the Somali first, then the sense: "Sida maahmaahdu tiraahdo, 'Far keliya fool ma dhaqdo' – qofna kaligiis wax ma qabsan karo"; (3) one proverb per reply is plenty; (4) some old proverbs about women, clans or social groups are offensive today – avoid them unless the user is studying them. Proverbs are traditional oral literature; Somali text is given as recorded in the cited collections (spelling lightly standardised). English glosses and usage notes are written fresh for this library.
Sources: https://www.ling.upenn.edu/courses/Spring_1998/ling202/proverbs.htm; https://muslimsinafrica.wordpress.com/2013/06/26/somali-proverbs (Somali proverbs largely from G. Kapchits' collections); Kapchits, Georgi (2012). Soomaali been ma maahmaahdo / Somalis do not lie in proverbs. Pisa: Ponte Invisibile (cited, not quoted); https://arcadia.sba.uniroma3.it/handle/2307/2164 (Kapchits, Qaamuuska Maahmaahyada Soomaaliyeed, 1988)
